**Major trends in microeconomics since  1930s** 

• So far we have covered 

– neoclassical microeconomics of A. Marshall and L. Walras  

– development of General Equlibrium Theory in the 20th century  (along with Formalist Revolution)  

• Its rise and glory – 

1\) a rigorous proof of the existence of general equlibrium (Arrow\&Debreu 1954);  

2\) proof that competitive equilibrium is Pareto optimal (Arrow, Debreu,  1950s).  

• Decline – 

1\) no general positive results on stability of general equilibrium;  2\) Sonnenschein-Mantel-Debreu theorem (1970s) – you cannot build sensible  macroeconomic theories on microfundations from General Equilibrium  Theory   
Major trends in microeconomics since 1930s 

• But there was also a different sort of microeconomics originating not  from Walras’s GET, but from A. Marshall’s partial equilibrium theory  

• This approach usually used less advanced mathematical formalisms  than GET and was used in introductory/intermediate textbooks  

• It evolved through a series of controversies to emerge circa 1955 as a  ‘neoclassical synthesis’ in microeconomics  

• A consensus on several microeconomic issues had been established  
Neoclassical synthesis in microeconoimcs – ca 1955 

Six main components  

1\. Competitive equilibrium, involving price-taking and free entry/exit  

2\. Demand determined by consumers, who maximize an ordinal  utility function subject to budget constraints  

3\. Consumers’ preferences are rational: complete and transitive  

4\. Firms behave as if they maximize profit subject to a production  function and prices of factors and products  

5\. Non-competitive behaviour means agents can influence price  

6\. Individual welfare functions without inter-personal comparability  of utility; Pareto-efficiency as welfare criterion  
Consumers and demand, 1930s-1950s 

• Widely accepted: demand is determined by consumers, who  maximize utility subject to budget constraints  

• But no consensus on what is utility?  

• Marshall (1920): utility measures intensity of human desires;  psychological interpretation of utility; utility can be (roughly)  measured in a cardinal way and compared accross persons  

• Pareto (1906): utility is not necessary for construction of demand  theory; economics is independent of psychology  

• In 1930s economists increasingly moved away from psychological  interpretations of utility  
Consumers and demand, 1930s-1950s 

• Lioner Robbins at LSE attacked (1932) Marshallian theory, arguing  that there is no scientific basis for interpersonal comparisons of  utility (ICU)  

• ICU rejected in mainstream demand theory and welfare economics  for the next (at least) 50 years  

• John Hicks and Roy Allen also at LSE (1934) took up program started  by Robbins (with Pareto as a precursor)  

• Hicks and Allen reformulated value and demand theory in terms of  MRS and ordinal utility functions – less demanding kind of  measurement, movement away from restrictive psychological  premises of older microeconomics  
Consumers and demand, 1930s-1950s 

• Next, in an even bolder move Paul Samuelson (1938) sought to  reduce consumer theory exclusively to what could be deduced from  axioms about observed choices  

• Gets rid of the assumption of ordinal utility functions  • Provides the same predictions as Hicks-Allen theory  • Called revealed preference theory  

• So, by 1940s economists abandoned psychological foundations  (concepts, premises) for microeconomics, focusing instead on  observed facts.  
Market structure and supply – 1930s-1950s 

• In 1920s Marshallian theories ruled – close to perfect competition  model (firms as price takers, free entry/exit)  

• Questioned in late 1920s and 1930s  

• Joan Robinson (1933) used new conceptual tools (like MR) to create  modern models of perfect and imperfect competition (monopoly,  monopsony, kinked demand curve etc.)  

• Edward Chamberlin (1933) introduced duopoly, oligopoly models and  monopolistic competition model  
Market structure and supply – 1930s-1950s 

• Chamberlin assumed product differentiation and selling costs (e.g.  advertising) – so perfect competition no longer describes the way in  which markets work  

• His work opened up the field of market structure  

• When drawing conlusions about efficiency of a particular market,  economists, first, analyzed empirically its structure, and only then  they applied a proper model  

• In theory, perfect competition model was treated as a general,  paradigmatic case (monopoly for use in specific cases), while  imperfect competition models largely swept to the field of industrial  organization (originated in 1940s)  
Market structure and supply – 1930s-1950s 

• Given the emphasis on imperfect competition in 1930s, why  microeconomics stabilized around the concept of perfect  competition?  

1\. General results (equilibrium prices, quantities) are hard to find in  theories of oligopoly and imperfect competition – destructive  consequences for economics in terms of predictive power  

2\. Progress in GET, taking place at the same time 1940s on, centered  on models constructed in perfect competition setting. From 1950s  on, it came to be regarded as the most rigorous version of  mainstream microeconomics  
Microeconomics since the mid-1980s: from  dominance of GET to moderate pluralism 

• GET occupied the dominant position since early 1950s  

• Negative results in 1970s (stability, SMD theorem) forced economists  to move away from GET  

• But it was not completely abandoned, still a very important and  active field of resarch (but not dominant anymore)  

• These developments took place on theoretical front – in practice,  texbooks, applied research etc. – GET (often implicitly) still persists as  the best approach  

• In microeconomic theory other approaches arose in the early- to  mid-1980s, and a stage of moderate pluralism has occured  
Microeconomics since the mid-1980s: game  theory 

• In mid-1980s the most prominent of the pluralist approaches became  rational choice game theory  

• **Rational choice game theory** – agents maximize given objective.  Contrasts with rule-following approaches such as evolutionary game  theory.  

• Attempts to mathematically capture behaviour in strategic situations,  in which an individual's success (payoff) in making choices depends  on the choices of others.  

• Traditional applications of game theory attempt to find equilibria  (solutions) in these games—sets of strategies in which individuals are  unlikely to change their behaviour  
Rational choice game theory 

• Nash equilibrium – each player is making the best decision that  she/he can, taking into account the decisions of the others  

• John Nash (b. 1928), won Nobel Prize in economics in 1994 with  Reinhard Selten and John Harsanyi 

• Game theory came into being with the 1944 book Theory of Games  and Economic Behaviour by John von Neumann and Oskar  Morgenstern  

• Major progress in 1950s and later, many applications to economics:  auctions, bargaining, duopolies, fair division, oligopolies, social  networks formation, voting systems etc.  

• Also applied in biology, political science, computer science,  philosophy etc  
John Nash (1928-2015)![][image1]  
![][image2]  
Rational choice game theory 

• Game theory gained enormous momentum in late 1980s – became  premier fashionable tool of microtheorists and dominated both  theory and applied research.  

• Transformed many fields: e.g. industrial organization, international  economics.  

• Unfortunately, rational choice game theory suffered from key  foundational problems:  

– common knowledge assumptions about how to play games (each player  knows each player’s rationality system, her strategies, and the structure of the  game).  

– Very implausible, unrealistic  

– assumptions and results were shown to be incompatible with experimental  evidence (some players simply do not maximize in an experimental setting)  
Game theory in economics since around 1990 

• Since around 1990 there was a turn toward evolutionary game  theory (EGT)  

• Agents are rule following (maximizing becomes only one possible rele of behaviour; other possibility – satisfying of a certain level)  

• Rejects neoclassical assumptions that agents are rational – preferences do not have to be transitive or complete  

• In EGT populations of agents evolve as more successful types (with  given rules of behaviour) replace (are imitated by) less successful  ones  

• Equilibrium is acheived if populations with different rules of  behaviour are stabilized.  
Game theory in economics since around 1990 

• Game theory involves a two-step move from traditional neoclassical  microeconomics:  

1\. Rational choice game theory adds interactivity to neoclassical  micro, but keeps rationality  

2\. EGT removes rationality (fundamental premise of neoclassicals)  

• So, EGT constitutes a great departure from neoclassical  microeconomics – probably paradigm-changing, revolutionary  development.   
Example of strategic interactions 

• The prisoners’ dilemma, 

• Mixing moves, 

• Strategic moves.  
Experimental economics 

• Another example of current moderate pluralism in microeconomics  following the demise of GET is experimental economics  

• Uses laboratory and field experiments to evaluate predictions from  economic theories; empirically oriented  

• Impresive rise since the mid-1980s  

• Started in 1950s, but ignored in the mainstream (1950s1980s)  dominated by axiomatic deductive methods  

• Vernon Smith (b. 1927), pioneer and leader, Nobel Prize (with Daniel  Kahneman) in economics  

• Experimental method is by nature inductive – collects pieces of  evidence to confirm or falsify economic theories  
Experimental economics 

• Like evolutionary game theory, experimental economics departs from  rationality postulate neoclassical economics  

• Axiom of transitive preferences was falsified in experiments as early  as in 1954\.  

• But in 1950s-1980s when deductive axiomatic approaches  dominated in economics experimental evidence was considered as  weak, soft, much less reliable (almost unscientific).  

• Today – growing popularity, many applications in analyses of working  of markets, bargaining, auctions, learning, tastes for fairnes/altruism,  decision making and many others  

• Limited to microeconomic applications  
Summary of major trends in 20th century  microeconomics 

• Many transformations of microeconomics in the 20th century:  

– interwar pluralism (many versions on neoclassical economics,  institutional economics, Marxian economics, Austrian school etc.)  

– dominance of mainstream economics based on axiomatic GET  (1950s-1980s)  

– moderate pluralism from 1990s on (GET, two versions of game  theory, experimental economics, and also behavioural economics,  neuroeconomics etc)  
Public Choice Theory  

• James M. Buchanan (1919 – 2013\) 

• Alfred Nobel Memorial Prize winner in Economic  Sciences in 1986\. 

• Professor Emeritus of Economics at George Mason  University and Philosophy at Virginia Polytechnic  Institute and State University. ![][image3]  
Public Choice Theory 

•He is best known for developing the “public choice theory” of economics, which changed the way economists analyze economic and political decision making. 

•Nations emerging from World War II, including the Western democracies, were allocating between one-third and one-half of their total product through political institutions rather than through markets.  
Public Choice Theory 

•Initially, the work of economists in this area raised serious doubts about the political process. • Kenneth Arrow and Duncan Black proved that democratic state by majority rule, could not work to promote any general or public interest.  
Public Choice Theory 

• The famous “impossibility theorem,” as published in Arrow’s book Social Choice and Individual Values (1951), stimulated an extended discussion. 

• The suggestion of this analysis was that majoritarian democracy is inherently unstable.  
Public Choice Theory 

•He entered the discussion with a generalized  critique of the analysis generated by the Arrow Duncan Black approach. 

• Aren’t “majority cycles” the most desirable  outcome of a democratic process?  

•Any attainment of political equilibrium via majority  rule would amount to the permanent burden on  the outvoted minority.   
Public Choice Theory 

•His concern, then and later, was the prevention of discrimination against minorities rather than stability of political outcomes. 

• The question, from an economist’s perspective, was how to obtain a combination of efficiency and justice under majority rule.  
**Meaning:** 

•Application of economics to the analysis of non market decision-making involving public goods, externalities and income distribution. 

•Application of economics to political science. • Economic analysis of politics.  
• Economics that studies the way that government makes decisions viz., level of taxes, public consumption and the size of transfer payments 

•It focuses on the problem of aggregating individual preferences to maximize a social welfare function. •Joseph Schumpeter was the pioneer in this area.  
• Followed by Antony Downs advanced this theory in  the private sector, consumers tend to maximize  utility and producers maximize profit. 

• Like that politicians tend towards or set economic  policies in order to be re-elected.  

• This theory was further advanced by J.M.  Buchanan. 

• Leader of the new institutional economists in  applying the economic way of thinking to the  political process.  
•In 1962 J.M. Buchanan and Gorden Tullock wrote a  book on ‘The Calculus of Consent’. 

•In this book, traditional analysis of political choice has individuals seek not to maximize his own utility,  but to find the “public interest” or “common good”  and the shift of an activity from the realm of private  to that of social choice involved the replacement of  the motive of private gain by that of social good.   
•In the modern politics, people do not change when they  move from their own private realm to that of politics. •Individual citizens, government officials (bureaucrats)  and politicians are guided by the self-interest. • Adam smith’s invisible hand is also at work in the  political system. 

• Each individual attempts to further his or her own  interests in political activities. 

• Parties formulate policies in order to win elections,  rather than win elections in order to formulate policies.  – Anthony Downs  
Scope of public choice: 

The theory of public choice covers a wider range of issues such as the whole gamut of public administration, property rights, the election process, voter behaviour, the role of independent judiciary, judicial activism, behaviour of legislators and government.  
Political Decision Making: 

•Decisions are made by elected representatives are  based on set of rules (constitution) and voting  system.   
**Players of political decision making;**    
**i.Voters:** like consumers in the market economy.  They tend to vote for candidates who favour  policies that will further their own individual  interests.    
However, voters much less informed about political  decisions than about their individual market  decisions. The lack of information is referred to as  rational ignorance.  
Players of political decision making;  

• Consumers have strong incentive to gain good information  about product. Exa. car or cell phone.  

• Voter have little incentive to gain good information about  candidates. They are rationally ignorant who may be called  as irrational voters.  

• Consumers compare prices to income and only buy those  products they are able to pay for. 

• Voters plan on other taxpayers paying for the voters’ wants.  • Thus the benefits (dams, roads) of political goods are visible  but costs are usually hidden.   
Players of Political Decision Making  

ii. **Politicians or Elected Representatives** like the firm in  market economy; they are the entrepreneur who  interpret the public’s demand for collective goods and  also find ways of supplying them. 

• Politicians seeks to maximize chance of reelection. They  are vote maximizers, just as firms are profit maximizers.   
Players of Political Decision Making  

**iii. Bureaucrats: (Administrative officers)** 

• Bureaucrats are the government agencies that carryout  the policies enacted by government. 

• Earn salary, promotions, and benefits 

• Gain support from colleagues 

•Influence decisions 

• Maintain power  
Players of Political Decision Making  

• **iv. Special- Interest Groups:** 

• Between voters and politicians are interest group. They  are organized to lobby for a specific set of interests or  issues. These pressure groups or organized lobbies seek to  elect politicians who support their cause.   
Players of Political Decision Making  

• Tariffs on steel 

• Rent controls in some cities 

• Sugar quotas 

• Milk prices 

• Farm Subsidies 

• In India, the farmer’s lobby having great influence over Member of  Parliament.   
Public Choice Theory 

• “Like the game of markets, the game of politics must match up  people’s demands for collective goods with the economy’s capability  to supply them.” 

• The major difference is that the central players of politics – politicians  – are primarily concerned with winning elections, while the major  players in markets – business firms – aim to earn profits.  
Mechanism for Public Choice: 

• Political system of a country makes collective decision. • In a democratic country, decision process is based on voting  system. 

• Public choice is the process by which preference of  individuals are combined into collective decisions. • In democratic societies the individualistic importance of  democracy is expressed in ‘one person, one vote’ system. • But the real problem in public choice is to aggregate millions  of opinions into a single decision.  
Mechanism for Public Choice: 

•In India there are about a billion views about any  issue. For example, about automic weaponisation. • Since, political choice is indivisible, these millions of  opinions have to be expressed in only one collective  decision – to weaponise or not to weaponise. • There is an element of coercion in such decision.  •In the market economy, private choice is not  coercive – my choice to eat rice does not affect your  consumption decision.   
Collective Decision Making: 

•Benefits of public goods for individual consumers  are the crucial problem for the government.  •But for small groups through mutual consultation it  is possible to determine what public good to  produce and what the contribution of each tax payer consumer will be.  
Collective Decision Making: 

• This is applicable in the case of services provided by  village panchayats and municipalities. But less  practical in the case of large groups involving  millions of consumers. Another problem is the  contribution of each taxpayer is very small, almost  nil, to the total cost and mutual consultation among  such a large group is not possible. 

•In such situation individual preferences are to be  translated into budget determination through the  political process and they are recorded as individual  preferences through voting.  
Conclusion 

• Let us be careful not to claim too much, however.  Public choice did not emerge from some profoundly  new insight, some new discovery, some social  science miracle. Public choice, in its basic insights  into the workings of politics, incorporates an  understanding of human nature that differs little.  The essential wisdom of the 18th century, of Adam  Smith and classical political economy was lost  through two centuries of intellectual folly. Public  choice does little more than incorporate a  rediscovery of this wisdom and its implications into  economic analyses of modern politics.
